hook: An image generator can show you twenty years from now, but first you have to describe who you will be.
lede: Young people choosing a career weigh desirability, money and personal interest, often with little information, and the tools they are given rarely show what a path might look like over time. When we asked students to picture their future selves with GenAI, many were unsure what they wanted, and the images they did get felt impersonal. Future Calling turns the prompt into a conversation: a career advisor chatbot gets to know the user, and an envisioner writes four linked chapters of a possible working life, one, five, ten and twenty years ahead, each with a story, a career path and an image carrying the user’s own face. We watched 20 young adults use it to explore, compare and question their futures.

chapters.title: Pictures without a story
paragraphs: We began with individual workshops with 19 university students aged 18–23. After a 10-minute demonstration of Stable Diffusion WebUI with Faceswaplab, each generated images of their own appearance, lifestyle and career one year and twenty years ahead, thinking aloud as they worked.

Many were unsure of their long-term goals and found it hard to write detailed prompts. The images that came back were described as “lacking a story” or “feeling impersonal”; one participant compared them to subway ads. Yet many said that seeing a future self reduced their anxiety and raised their confidence, and some played with unconventional careers, becoming superheroes or national leaders. Those findings shaped three features: guided prompt generation, narrative-driven visualizations and interactive chatbot support.

quote.text: I don’t even know what I want to do next year, let alone in 20 years.

figures.caption: What the workshops surfaced: difficulty envisioning future selves and a need for stories behind the images, alongside reduced anxiety and imaginative play.

chapters.title: An advisor who writes the prompt
paragraphs: Future Calling is a web application built on GPT-4, DALL-E 3 and the Baidu FaceSwap API. Users upload a photo and basic details, then talk with the Career Advisor, a GPT-4 chatbot prompted to draw out their interests and experiences in a gentle, encouraging and professional tone, suggesting occupations along the way. From the conversation it keeps refining a user profile, so users no longer have to write image prompts themselves.

When a user types in an occupation, the Future Envisioner combines it with the profile and writes three interrelated elements for each of four stages: a future story, a career path and a description for a future image. A first chapter might begin, “Year 1: You start as a digital content creator, focusing on historical topics.” DALL-E 3 renders each image and the face-swap service replaces the generated face with the user’s own. Any image, story or path can be regenerated with feedback, and users can return to try another occupation.

figures.caption: Two modules: the Career Advisor concludes a user profile from conversation, and the Future Envisioner uses it to generate images, stories and career paths that users can regenerate with new prompts.

chapters.title: Four careers, side by side
paragraphs: Twenty participants recruited from universities in China, 10 undergraduates, 6 graduate students and 4 early-career professionals, each used Future Calling for around 30 minutes while thinking aloud, with surveys before and after and an interview at the end.

P8 had a political science background and an interest in design. The advisor suggested several paths; she chose illustrator, then went on to generate three more careers and compare them side by side. Along the way she asked how to balance realistic expectations with ideals, and put a harder question to the advisor: “If I don’t like the job of a political science teacher in real work, do I need to compromise for practical economic reasons?” She finished by asking how the careers’ incomes differed.

Participants still exploring behaved like P8: she and P3 each generated four career plans. Those with an established direction usually generated one and asked specific questions instead, about salaries or exam requirements. “I’m only interested in my current research field and want to know how I can develop in this area,” said P6.

quote.text: I love to use the Future Envisioner to search and generate different careers. In this way, I can compare how they develop.

figures.caption: P8 moved back and forth between four envisioned careers (illustrator, florist, fashion designer and political teacher) and the Career Advisor, asking which suited her and what each would earn.

chapters.title: Correcting a future that is not yours
paragraphs: Much of the reflection happened in the edits. When a story showed P6 conducting daily lab experiments, he objected, “That’s not possible; it’s not like me,” and rewrote what he wanted to do. He also added a contingency: “What if I lose the job?” P2 wrote a master’s degree into her five-year story, and P10 aligned his path with policies such as the Belt and Road Initiative.

P11, an engineering student, refined two careers in depth. He corrected and extended the generated career paths, asked for “more details,” worked in networking advice the advisor had given him earlier, and regenerated the image of himself ten years on, until the plan reflected his own information and goals.

quote.text: It’s like I’m starting to understand myself, what I like and don’t like, and the choices I’m going to make.

figures.caption: P11 refined two pathways, “Institute members of central enterprises” and “Tech entrepreneur and self-media blogger on technology,” by conversing with the advisor and regenerating stories, paths and images with new prompts.

chapters.title: A goal, and the steps toward it
paragraphs: Pairing each goal with concrete advice changed how reachable it felt. P2, who wants to be an algorithm engineer, saw a ten-year goal of becoming a senior engineer in machine learning and leading a multinational team, paired with steps: attend international conferences, join multinational projects, expand her network, lead small projects. For P10, a one-year suggestion to look for internships at internet companies lined up with a five-year goal of working at a leading gaming company.

Distance cut both ways. “AI can create a very long-term career plan and make the final goal seem less distant,” said P1. But P10, whose story began with him teaching dance within a year, found the far end harder to accept: “I feel that the 20-year vision is a bit unreasonable, and I doubt this career will achieve such milestones in 20 years.”

Across all 20 participants, career self-efficacy rose significantly after using Future Calling (d = 0.652, p = .009). Career maturity, which also depends on outside factors such as career education and real-world experience, improved only marginally (d = 0.447, p = .06).

quote.text: If I only looked at the career goal, it would just be an imagination for me, but effective career advice makes it seem achievable!

figures.caption: P2’s ten-year story and the career advice beneath it: the goal alone felt like imagination, the steps made it seem achievable.

chapters.title: Too successful to believe
paragraphs: The envisioned futures leaned bright. A user who mentioned wanting to work at a tech company would often appear, twenty years on, as a highly prominent figure. For P3 that was fuel: “It might be a little too positive, but it’s not bad—it gives me confidence. When I think of this kind of life, I want to start studying right now!” For others it bred doubt about whether such idealized futures were reachable. Some images also reinforced stereotypes, such as professionals always dressed in suits, and some participants found the information of limited use: “The information was all searchable on the internet and of little value,” said P5.

Some participants asked for less idealized, even negative, scenarios as a heads-up for what lies ahead; P3 wanted the AI to be “like a senior telling you about the pitfalls and challenges you might face at different stages of your career.” That points to next steps: retrieval of specific career information for users with clear goals, stricter prompting or fine-tuning to keep futures closer to where users are now, and an AI that asks, “What kind of impact do you hope to make through your work?” rather than declaring which career fits.

quote.text: It’s too successful. It sounds so simple, but every step can be unsuccessful, every step takes chance and luck.

takeaways: An image of a future self felt impersonal on its own; paired with a story and step-by-step advice, it made career goals feel achievable.
Reflection happened in the corrections: editing futures that did not fit pushed participants to say what they actually wanted.
Overly positive futures motivated some participants and raised doubts in others, so career tools may need balanced scenarios and questions rather than verdicts.

facts.label: System
facts.value: React web app; GPT-4 Career Advisor; DALL-E 3 and Baidu FaceSwap API for the Future Envisioner

facts.label: User study
facts.value: 20 participants aged 18–25; pre- and post-surveys, a ~30-minute session with think-aloud, and interviews

facts.label: Limitations
facts.value: Outcomes measured only immediately after use; young adults only; GPT-4 content often general and positive; DALL-E 3 images reflected narrow professional stereotypes
